## Maturity model levels

* Level 0: None, Never, Negligible, Not Applicable.
* Level 1: Initiate, Investigate, Implicit, Individual-oriented, Informal-usage.
* Level 2: Develop, Describe, Duplicate, Direct-oriented, Department-usage.
* Level 3: Standardize, Specify, Scale, Service-oriented, Segment-usage.
* Level 4: Manage, Measure, Mainstream, Mission-oriented, Mass-usage.
* Level 5: Orchestrate, Optimize, Originate, Opportunity-oriented, Outsize-usage.

## How to use this model

* Score each practice area independently. A health service is typically level 4 in one area and level 1 in another, and that unevenness is the useful signal.
* Score what is evidenced, not what is aspired to. If a control exists but produces no artifact, treat it as the level below.
* Read the levels as cumulative. Level 4 assumes the level 3 standards still hold, and level 5 assumes the level 4 measures still run.
* Treat regulated areas differently. For clinical and device practice areas, a jump from level 1 to level 3 without the intervening governance work is a safety risk, not a shortcut.
* Re-score on a fixed cadence, such as annually, so the model measures trajectory rather than a single moment.

Other parts of the organisation take different directions.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A directorate publishes an AI strategy that other directorates do not follow.<br>2. A data science team is formed in one organisation with no shared platform.<br>3. Skills gaps are described in a paper but not funded. | An engineering operating model is specified across the organisation or region: platform teams, service ownership, architecture principles that include AI, and defined career paths.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Architecture principles mandate a governed model gateway, an evaluation harness, and monitoring for any AI service.<br>2. A platform team owns shared AI services so product teams do not each rebuild them.<br>3. Engineering job families, progression, and pay bands are defined and published. | Engineering leadership is measured and accountable at board level. Delivery, capability, and build-versus-buy decisions are evidenced rather than asserted.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Delivery metrics such as deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and restoration time are reported to the board.<br>2. A named executive holds explicit accountability for AI outcomes and risks in the boardroom.<br>3. Recruitment, retention, and internal capability growth are tracked against a workforce plan. | Engineering leadership extends beyond the organisation. Shared platforms, open source, and talent pipelines are orchestrated across the health system, and the organisation sets direction rather than following it.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A shared regional platform serves multiple organisations instead of each maintaining its own.<br>2. Reusable components are open-sourced and their reuse by peers is tracked and supported.<br>3. Apprenticeships, academic partnerships, and clinical-technical hybrid roles build a sustained pipeline. |
| **System leadership of medical practitioners** | Clinicians have no leadership role in AI. Decisions are made by technology and procurement functions, and clinical risk ownership is undefined.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. No chief clinical or nursing information officer role exists.<br>2. No certified clinical safety officer is appointed for digital deployments.<br>3. Clinicians first learn about an AI tool when it appears in their workflow. | An enthusiastic individual clinician advocates for AI without job-planned time, mandate, or a governance route. Their projects live and die with their goodwill.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A consultant runs AI evaluations in their own unpaid time.<br>2. There is no route from their project into clinical governance.<br>3. Colleagues are unaware the work is happening. | A department appoints a digital clinical lead with described responsibilities and some protected time. Influence is limited to that department.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A directorate clinical lead has job-planned sessions for digital work.<br>2. A local route into the directorate governance meeting is described.<br>3. One local training session on AI is delivered to a specialty team. | Clinical digital leadership is specified organisation-wide, with named senior clinical information roles, certified clinical safety officers, AI standing in clinical governance, and explicit statements of professional accountability.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A certified clinical safety officer with job-planned time is required for every AI deployment.<br>2. AI performance and incidents are a standing item in clinical governance and clinical audit.<br>3. Policy states plainly that clinical accountability for a decision stays with the clinician regardless of AI involvement. | Clinical leadership is measured on the things that matter: clinician confidence, appropriate reliance, override behaviour, training, and safety outcomes across the whole workforce.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Automation-bias audits sample cases where clinicians agreed with and overrode AI output, and look for inappropriate deference.<br>2. AI literacy is embedded in mandatory training, appraisal, and continuing professional development.<br>3. Clinician-reported experience of AI tools is surveyed and acted on, with results published internally. | Clinical leaders shape the field beyond their own organisation, through research, guideline development, professional standards, and evaluation networks.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A clinical academic partnership prospectively evaluates deployed AI and publishes the results, including negative findings.<br>2. Clinicians contribute to national guidelines and professional body positions on AI in practice.<br>3. Clinical AI fellowships and secondments build a pipeline of clinically credible digital leaders. |
| **System leadership of government stakeholders** | There is no engagement with government, regulators, or national bodies on AI. Public accountability for AI use is undefined.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. No reporting on AI reaches the sponsoring department or national body.<br>2. The organisation does not respond to policy consultations.<br>3. There is no funding strategy for AI beyond opportunistic bids. | Individuals respond to consultations or talk to national contacts informally. Positions are personal and uncoordinated.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. One executive answers a call for evidence without internal sign-off.<br>2. An informal relationship with a national programme lead is the only channel.<br>3. Two parts of the organisation give national bodies contradictory information. | The organisation describes its position and briefs stakeholders occasionally, usually around a specific bid or visit. Engagement is reactive.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A briefing pack is produced for a visiting politician or national official.<br>2. A benefits case is written to support one national funding bid.<br>3. The organisation joins a national pilot without a plan for what happens after it. | Engagement is specified and routine: published transparency records, defined reporting lines to national bodies and regulators, board-level accountability for AI, and deliberate alignment to national strategy and funding conditions.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Algorithmic transparency records are published for public-facing AI as a matter of standard practice.<br>2. Reporting routes to the sponsoring department, the device regulator, and the data protection authority are defined and rehearsed.<br>3. Local AI plans are explicitly mapped to national digital and data strategy commitments. | Performance is measured against national frameworks, benchmarked against peers, and subject to independent external scrutiny that the organisation can evidence.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. The organisation benchmarks itself through national digital maturity assessments and acts on the gaps.<br>2. External audit and parliamentary or public scrutiny is met with prepared evidence rather than improvisation.<br>3. An annual public report covers AI use, benefits, incidents, and equity impact. | The organisation co-creates policy, standards, and funding models, works internationally, and helps shape the rules that everyone else will follow.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Staff sit on regulator sandboxes, standards committees, and national advisory groups.<br>2. International collaboration shares evaluation methods and real-world evidence across health systems.<br>3. The organisation helps design national procurement frameworks and payment models for AI. |
| **Digital sovereignty** | Where data is processed, who can access it, and under whose law is never asked. Defaults are whatever the supplier offers.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Contracts contain no data residency or jurisdiction clause.<br>2. Subprocessors and their locations are unknown and unlisted.<br>3. Nobody can say which country a given inference request is served from. | An individual raises the question and investigates informally. There is concern but no requirement, register, or decision.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. An architect asks a supplier where inference happens and receives a vague answer.<br>2. A project notes an international data transfer without completing a transfer risk assessment.<br>3. No register of cross-border data flows exists. | One department writes residency requirements into a single contract and drafts transfer assessments. Practice is duplicated case by case rather than set as policy.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. One contract requires in-country storage but is silent on processing and support access.<br>2. A transfer risk assessment is drafted for a single supplier.<br>3. A stated preference for local hosting exists with no enforcement mechanism. | Sovereignty requirements are specified for every AI system: data residency, jurisdictional control, subprocessor transparency, key management, and evidenced portability and exit.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Patient data is processed in-country under domestic law, including support and administrative access paths.<br>2. Encryption keys are customer-managed and revocable, so a supplier cannot read data unilaterally.<br>3. An approved model list records hosting location, jurisdiction, and retention terms for each option. | Sovereignty risk is measured and managed as a strategic risk: concentration, dependency, and lock-in are quantified and reported, and exit is rehearsed rather than theoretical.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A live register records every cross-border transfer with its lawful basis and safeguards.<br>2. Supplier and model concentration risk is quantified and reported to the board alongside other strategic risks.<br>3. Exit and portability tests are executed on a schedule, including extraction of prompts, configurations, and fine-tuning assets. | The organisation has genuine strategic autonomy. Workloads move between providers without service loss, open and sovereign options are viable, and shared public infrastructure reduces dependency.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Critical AI workloads are proven portable across at least two providers with measured switch time.<br>2. Open-weight models running on national or regional compute are validated as credible alternatives for defined use cases.<br>3. The organisation contributes to and consumes shared public AI infrastructure rather than duplicating private stacks. |
| **Upskilling** | No AI training exists. The workforce is unprepared, and nobody knows what the baseline skill level is.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Induction and mandatory training contain no AI or data literacy content.<br>2. No digital skills baseline has ever been measured.<br>3. There is no training budget line for AI.| Individuals teach themselves in their own time and at their own expense. Skill is concentrated in a few enthusiasts and invisible to workforce planning.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A clinician completes an online AI course unfunded and outside working hours.<br>2. Informal lunchtime sessions are run by whoever is interested.<br>3. No record exists of who has been trained in what. | A department builds a curriculum for its own staff and tracks completion locally. Quality varies and nothing transfers between departments.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A directorate runs AI awareness sessions for its own teams only.<br>2. A local champions network forms without a defined role or time allocation.<br>3. Completion is tracked in a spreadsheet held by the department. | A role-based curriculum is specified for the whole workforce, with defined competencies, mandatory foundations, protected time, and assessment, aligned to recognised capability frameworks.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Tiered pathways serve all staff, frequent users, builders, and approvers, each with defined competencies.<br>2. AI and data literacy is part of induction and mandatory training for every role.<br>3. Protected learning time is job-planned rather than expected to happen in gaps. | Capability is measured, not attendance. Competence, confidence, and safe applied use are assessed across the whole workforce and drive targeted intervention.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Competence is assessed through practical scenarios, including recognising when not to trust an AI output.<br>2. Capability data by staff group and site identifies where to invest next.<br>3. Training coverage is correlated with AI-related incidents and unsafe-use reports. | Learning is orchestrated as a continuous system embedded in work, with fellowships, academic partnerships, and curricula exported to the wider health system.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. In-workflow coaching surfaces guidance at the moment of use rather than in a classroom months earlier.<br>2. AI fellowships and secondments rotate staff between clinical, technical, and governance roles.<br>3. Curricula and assessment materials are shared with other organisations and education providers. |
| **Redundancies** | Workforce impact is not considered. Business cases claim savings without stating whether posts are affected, and no consultation or redeployment thinking exists.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. An AI business case claims a cash-releasing saving without naming any affected role.<br>2. No workforce impact assessment template exists.<br>3. Staff representatives are not involved in AI decisions at any stage. | Individual managers speculate and act informally. Anxiety spreads through rumour, which damages adoption more than the technology ever would.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Rumours circulate that AI will cut administrative posts, with no official statement.<br>2. A manager quietly freezes a vacancy in anticipation of automation.<br>3. Staff hide their own AI use for fear of automating their own role away. | A department describes expected workforce impact in a business case and handles consequences case by case. Consultation starts late, after decisions are effectively made.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A directorate business case states a number of posts released without specifying which roles or how.<br>2. A few staff are redeployed informally through manager goodwill.<br>3. Formal consultation begins only once the technology is already contracted. | A specified policy requires workforce impact assessment before AI approval, redeployment-first handling, early consultation with staff representatives, and clear criteria distinguishing role change from redundancy.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A workforce impact assessment sits alongside data protection and equality impact assessments as a mandatory approval gate.<br>2. Policy commits that released time is first reinvested in care quality and backlog before any headcount decision.<br>3. Staff representatives are involved from design stage, not at notice stage. | Transitions are measured and managed. Redeployment success, equality impact, and whether predicted savings actually materialised are all tracked and reported.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. Redeployment rates and post-transition retention are tracked by staff group.<br>2. Equality impact of role changes is analysed by protected characteristic and acted on where disparities appear.<br>3. Post-implementation review tests whether claimed savings were realised or merely displaced elsewhere. | Workforce transition is orchestrated across the health system, using attrition and reskilling rather than displacement, and creating the new roles that AI itself requires.<br><br>Examples:<br>1. A regional employer network shares redeployment opportunities so staff move between organisations rather than out of the sector.<br>2. New roles such as AI assurance specialist, clinical safety officer, and prompt and evaluation engineer are created and funded.<br>3. The organisation publishes its workforce transition evidence so others can plan on real data rather than vendor claims. |

## Notes on scope

* **Redundancies** in this model means workforce reduction and role change arising from AI adoption. Operational redundancy in the engineering sense, meaning failover and fallback when a system or model is unavailable, is covered under **Software high availability** and **Software disaster recovery**.
* **System leadership** rows assess the leadership of a constituency, not the seniority of individuals. An organisation can employ excellent clinicians and still score level 1 on system leadership of medical practitioners if none of them has a mandate, protected time, or a governance route.
* **Digital sovereignty** is scored on demonstrated control and evidenced portability, not on stated preference. A contract clause requiring in-country storage is level 2 evidence; a rehearsed provider switch is level 5 evidence.
* **Software rows** are grouped together near the top of the table because they progress together. An organisation rarely reaches level 4 in **Software DevOps** while remaining at level 1 in **Software architecture**, and a mismatch between them is usually worth investigating.
* **Apps and websites** rows are split by audience because the safety, accessibility, and disclosure obligations differ sharply between patients and providers.
